q: Ohm's law (the current through a conductor is proportional to the p.d. across it) holds for a metal wire only if:
o: Its length is less than one metre
Its temperature and other physical conditions stay the same
The current flows for less than one second
The p.d. across it is less than 1 V
x: Ohm's law, V ∝ I, holds only while the temperature and other physical conditions of the conductor stay constant. Heating a wire changes its resistance; the wire's length and the time the current flows are not conditions of the law.

q: The reciprocal of resistance is called conductance. Its SI unit is the:
x: Conductance G = 1/R, so its unit is Ω⁻¹, named the siemens (S). The ohm metre is the unit of resistivity, not of conductance.

q: The current in a wire rises uniformly from 0 to 4 A in 10 s. The charge that passes a cross-section of the wire in these 10 s is:
x: Charge is the area under the current-time graph: a triangle, ½ × 10 s × 4 A = 20 C. The same follows from the average current 2 A × 10 s. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 C.

q: In a simple model of an atom, an electron moves round a circular orbit 5 × 10¹⁵ times per second. The equivalent current due to this motion is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):
x: The charge e passes any point of the orbit f times per second, so I = ef = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10¹⁵ = 8 × 10⁻⁴ A. Dividing e by f instead of multiplying gives 3.2 × 10⁻³⁵ A.

q: Wires P and Q have the same cross-sectional area and carry the same current. Metal P has three times as many free electrons per cubic metre as metal Q. The ratio of drift speeds, v(P) : v(Q), is:
x: From I = nAve, with I, A and e the same, v ∝ 1/n. So P's electrons drift at one-third of Q's speed: 1 : 3. Taking v proportional to n gives 3 : 1.

q: The p.d. across an ohmic resistor is increased by 50% while its resistance is reduced by 25%. The current, compared with its original value I, becomes:
x: I = V/R, so the new current is (1.5V)/(0.75R) = 2I. Multiplying the two factors (1.5 × 0.75) instead of dividing gives 1.125I; ignoring the change in R gives 1.5I.

q: A graph of current (vertical axis) against p.d. (horizontal axis) for a filament lamp curves over and bends towards the p.d. axis as the p.d. increases. This shows that the lamp's resistance:
o: Increases, because the filament gets hotter
Decreases, because the filament gets hotter
Stays constant, as for any metal
Falls to zero at high p.d.
x: R = V/I, and on this graph each step in V gives a smaller rise in I, so V/I grows. The hotter filament has more vibrating ions, so its resistance rises. A falling resistance would make the curve bend towards the current axis.

q: A uniform wire of resistance R draws a current I from a fixed p.d. V. The wire is cut into four equal pieces, which are then connected in parallel across the same p.d. V. The current drawn from the supply is now:
x: Each piece has resistance R/4; four of them in parallel give (R/4)/4 = R/16. With the same V, the current becomes 16I. Stopping after cutting (R/4) gives 4I.

q: The resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR):
o: Increases as the intensity of light falling on it increases
Does not depend on light, only on temperature
Decreases as the intensity of light falling on it increases
x: Light frees more charge carriers in the LDR's semiconductor, so its resistance falls in bright light and is very high in darkness.

q: A carbon resistor has colour bands red, red, brown and gold, in that order. Its actual resistance can lie anywhere between:
x: Red = 2, red = 2, brown multiplier = 10¹, so R = 22 × 10 = 220 Ω; gold means ±5%, which is ±11 Ω, giving 209 Ω to 231 Ω. Taking gold as ±10% gives 198-242 Ω; reading brown as two zeros gives 2090-2310 Ω.

q: An NTC thermistor is used as the temperature sensor in a fire alarm. It is suitable because, as its temperature rises, its resistance:
x: An NTC (negative temperature coefficient) thermistor is a semiconductor: heating frees more charge carriers, so its resistance falls steeply, giving a large change in current for a small rise in temperature.

q: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 4 Ω. The conductivity of its material is:
x: ρ = RA/L = 4 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, and conductivity σ = 1/ρ = 1 × 10⁶ S m⁻¹. Writing the resistivity's number with the conductivity unit gives 1 × 10⁻⁶ S m⁻¹.

q: A carbon resistor (temperature coefficient −5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) is connected in series with an iron wire (temperature coefficient +5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹). Their total resistance is 110 Ω and, for small temperature changes, does not change with temperature. The resistance of the carbon resistor is:
x: For no net change, the rise in the iron's resistance must cancel the fall in the carbon's: R(carbon) × 5 × 10⁻⁴ = R(iron) × 5 × 10⁻³, so R(carbon) = 10 R(iron). Then 11 R(iron) = 110 Ω gives R(iron) = 10 Ω and R(carbon) = 100 Ω. Swapping the two gives 10 Ω.

q: For a metal wire, resistance R is plotted against temperature θ in °C. The graph is a straight line, R = R₀(1 + αθ), where R₀ is the resistance at 0 °C. The gradient of this line equals:
x: R = R₀ + (αR₀)θ, a straight line of intercept R₀ and gradient αR₀. α alone is the gradient divided by the intercept.

q: Which of these materials has the smallest resistivity at room temperature?
x: Silver is the best metallic conductor. Nichrome is an alloy with a much higher resistivity, germanium is a semiconductor, and glass is an insulator.

q: One kilowatt-hour (the 'unit' on an electricity bill) is equal to:
An electric iron rated 500 W is used for 10 minutes. The electrical energy it uses is:
x: E = Pt = 500 W × (10 × 60) s = 3 × 10⁵ J. Leaving the time in minutes gives 5 × 10³ J.

q: A 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
o: The 100 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the higher power rating
The 60 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the larger resistance and the same current flows in both
Both glow equally, because the same current flows in both
The 100 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the larger resistance
x: R = V²/P, so the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance. In series the current is the same, and P = I²R is larger for the larger resistance, so the 60 W bulb is brighter. The rating applies only at the full 220 V across each bulb.

q: A heater takes power P from a fixed-voltage supply. Its coil is cut in half and only one half is connected to the same supply. Assuming the resistance does not change with temperature, the power taken is now:
x: Half the coil has resistance R/2, and P = V²/R with V fixed, so the power doubles to 2P. Using P = I²R with the old current gives P/2.

q: A cell drives a current of 1 A through an external 2 Ω resistor and a current of 0.5 A through an external 5 Ω resistor. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are:
x: E = I(R + r): E = 1 × (2 + r) and E = 0.5 × (5 + r). Equating, 2 + r = 2.5 + 0.5r, so r = 1 Ω and E = 3 V. Check: 3/(5 + 1) = 0.5 A. The other pairs fit only one of the two readings.

q: A battery of internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external load of 4 Ω. The fraction of the power produced by the battery that is delivered to the load is:
x: The same current flows through r and R, so the fraction is I²R / I²(R + r) = 4/5 = 80%. The 20% is the share wasted inside the battery.

q: A battery of emf 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged by a charger that drives a current of 2 A into its positive terminal. The p.d. across the battery's terminals during charging is:
x: During charging the current flows against the emf, so the charger must supply the emf plus the internal drop: V = E + Ir = 6 + 2 × 0.5 = 7 V. Subtracting Ir, as when the battery is discharging, gives 5 V.

q: Kirchhoff's first rule (the junction rule: the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it) is a consequence of the conservation of:
x: Charge cannot pile up or disappear at a junction, so the current in equals the current out: conservation of charge. The loop rule is the one based on conservation of energy.

q: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The total current drawn from the battery is:
x: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω and I = 6/1 = 6 A. Check: 3 A + 2 A + 1 A = 6 A. Adding the resistors as if in series (11 Ω) gives about 0.55 A.

q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in series, the 2 Ω resistor being joined to the positive terminal. Taking the negative terminal as 0 V, the potential of the junction between the two resistors is:
x: I = 12/6 = 2 A. Going from the positive terminal (12 V) through the 2 Ω resistor, the potential falls by 2 × 2 = 4 V, leaving 8 V; this is also the 8 V across the 4 Ω resistor. Taking the drop itself as the answer gives 4 V.

q: A 9 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination. One branch of the combination is a 6 Ω resistor; the other branch is a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in series. The p.d. across the 4 Ω resistor is:
x: The branches are 6 Ω and 6 Ω, so the combination is 3 Ω; the total is 6 Ω and I = 1.5 A. The p.d. across the combination is 4.5 V, so the 2 Ω + 4 Ω branch carries 0.75 A and the 4 Ω resistor has 0.75 × 4 = 3 V. 4.5 V is the p.d. across the whole branch.

q: A uniform wire of resistance 12 Ω is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between two points at opposite ends of a diameter is:
x: The two points split the circle into two semicircles of 6 Ω each, in parallel between them: 6 × 6/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω. Taking just one semicircle gives 6 Ω.

q: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series across a 3 Ω resistor, but one cell has been connected the wrong way round. The current in the resistor is:
x: The reversed cell cancels one correct cell, so the net emf is 3 × 1.5 − 1.5 = 3 V, but all four internal resistances (2 Ω) are still in the circuit: I = 3/(3 + 2) = 0.6 A. With all cells aiding, 6/5 = 1.2 A; treating the reversed cell as simply missing gives 4.5/5 = 0.9 A.

q: A 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 2 Ω resistor. The current in the 3 Ω resistor is 2 A. The p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor is:
x: The p.d. across the parallel pair is 2 × 3 = 6 V, so the 6 Ω resistor carries 1 A. The total current is 3 A, and the p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor is 3 × 2 = 6 V. Using only the 2 A in the 3 Ω resistor gives 4 V.

q: When a Wheatstone bridge is balanced, the two points joined by the galvanometer are:
o: At different potentials, so a large current flows through the galvanometer
Joined directly to the positive terminal of the battery
At the same potential, so no current flows through the galvanometer
At zero potential only when the battery is removed
x: Balance means zero galvanometer current, which happens only when there is no p.d. between its two ends: the two junctions are at equal potentials.

q: In a Wheatstone bridge, P and Q are in series in one branch and R and S in series in the other, both branches across a battery; a galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. The bridge is balanced. If the battery and the galvanometer are interchanged, the galvanometer:
o: Shows a deflection that depends on the battery's emf
x: The balance condition P/Q = R/S can be rewritten P/R = Q/S, which is exactly the balance condition with the battery and galvanometer swapped. So the bridge stays balanced.

q: In a metre bridge, resistor P is in the left gap and resistor Q in the right gap, and the balance point is 40 cm from the left end of the 100 cm wire. When a 5 Ω resistor is added in series with Q, the balance point moves to 30 cm from the left end. The value of P is:
x: P/Q = 40/60, so P = 2Q/3. Then P/(Q + 5) = 30/70, so 7P = 3Q + 15; substituting, 14Q/3 = 3Q + 15, giving Q = 9 Ω and P = 6 Ω. Check: 6/14 = 3/7. 9 Ω is Q, not P.

q: A potentiometer is used to measure the emf of a test cell, but no balance point can be found anywhere along the wire. A likely reason is that:
o: The emf of the driver cell is less than the emf of the test cell
The potentiometer wire is too long
The emf of the driver cell is much larger than that of the test cell
x: A balance needs some length of wire whose p.d. equals the test emf. If the whole wire's p.d., set by the driver cell, is smaller than the test emf, no point balances. A larger driver emf or a longer wire still gives a balance point.

q: A 6 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected across a fixed 2 kΩ resistor in series with a light-dependent resistor (LDR). The output is taken across the fixed resistor. In bright light the LDR's resistance is 1 kΩ. The output p.d. is:
x: Potential divider: V(out) = 6 × 2/(2 + 1) = 4 V. The 2 V is the p.d. across the LDR, not across the fixed resistor.

q: A potentiometer wire 2 m long of resistance 4 Ω is connected in series with a resistor R and a 2 V driver cell of negligible internal resistance. A thermocouple of emf 5 mV is balanced by 50 cm of the wire. The value of R is:
x: Gradient = 5 mV / 0.5 m = 10 mV m⁻¹, so the 2 m wire has 20 mV across it and the current is 0.02/4 = 5 mA. The p.d. across R is 2 − 0.02 = 1.98 V, so R = 1.98/0.005 = 396 Ω. 400 Ω is the total circuit resistance, before subtracting the wire's 4 Ω.

q: To measure a current with a potentiometer, the current is passed through a standard 2 Ω resistor and the p.d. across that resistor is balanced by 40 cm of potentiometer wire. The potential gradient of the wire is 0.01 V cm⁻¹. The current is:
x: V = 0.01 V cm⁻¹ × 40 cm = 0.4 V, so I = V/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A. Multiplying by R instead of dividing gives 0.8 A.
